The person who intends to make simply good butter will make it in such a way that there will not be 16 per cent of water in it. That is the way the ordinary dairy butter is made in this country by people even who make it by rule of thumb, and the result is that the butter they make if of good quality, does not contain as much as 14 per cent of water. When it goes to a larger percentage it is because somebody is attempting to put in as much water as he possibly can without making his butter bad, and in this he is liable to overstep the limits. However, I am perfectly willing to discuss this question and to investigate it, and I will do so before I bring in the Bill.
I would like to ask the hon. Minister of Agriculture if it is his intention to appoint butter inspectors 1
There is no intention to appoint inspectors to carry out this Bill ?
How are you going to carry it out ?

In regard to what the hon. member for South Brant (Mr. Heyd) has said, of course, the hon. Minister of Agriculture (Hon. Mr. Fisher) may introduce a Bill in such terms as will make any farmer liable for even an innocent violation of the law. There are examples of statute law requiring guilty knowledge and of other statutes not requiring it. I understand the observation of the hon. member for South Brant to be a little different from the hon. minister's understanding of it. I understand him to suggest that it might be quite possible for a farmer's wife to make butter of such a character that it would contain more than 16 per cent of water, and to do that quite innocently. The hon. gentleman supposed that an individual who was innocently violating the terms of the statute would not be subject to any penalty. That might be a matter for the consideration of the minister before lie brings in a Bill. In some cases motives of public policy have induced parliament to hold a man guilty and to make him liable to the penalty even where there is no intention whatever of violating the Act, because in such cases it is in the public interest that whether innocently or with guilty Hon. Mr. FISHER.
knowledge there should be a penalty for the violation of the terms of the statute!
Mr. SPROULE'. In regard to the hon. minister's opinion that this law could not be violated unless a person designedly intends to do it, I may say that I do not agree with his opinion as to the way in which a large percentage of water will be found in butter. When butter is churned, it is in granules, and between these granules the space is filled up largely with milk and whey, and water is put in to wash out the milk and whey. If this is properly worked on an inclined plane the water will run off. In the ordinary dairy, whether worked with a machine or on a tray, it is always on an inclined plane, and the water will run off. If it is not worked sufficiently it will contain a larger percentage of water and milk, and the reason why butter deteriorates rapidly is because of the large percentage of milk it contains. If that is well washed out it is purer and better butter and will contain a less percentage of water than it otherwise would. But, if butter is very little worked, and worked in some improper way, and the water is not constantly poured off, and the buttermilk washed off, then, it will contain a very much larger percentage of water and will be liable to be found to be in violation of the law. It is the careless butter maker who will be more likely to suffer, not from any design to put water into the butter, but from the fact that he did not work it enough to take out the water.

House in committee on following proposed resolution :
Resolved, that it is expedient to pass an Act providing that seeds of cereals, grasses, clovers, forage plants or vegetables, sold for the purpose of seeding, shall be free from the seeds of certain weeds ; establishing grades of seeds, of timothy, red clover, and alsike, and providing that such seeds offered for sale shall be marked with the seller's name and address, the name of the kind of seed, and the grade ; providing for the examination of such seeds, and their analysis by an official seed analyst ; and providing that one-half of the pecuniary penalties for contraventions of the Act shall be payable to the informant.
Would the hon. minister explain this ?

Mr. Chairman, this resolution comes up in consequence of the ruling of Mr. Speaker that the Bill which I introduced to the House and explained the other day, being a Bill dealing with trade in some of its provisions, must come in the form of a resolution. I explained the Bill the other day on its introduction and first reading. I would, therefore, ask the concurrence of the House in this resolution, so that we can

proceed again with the Bill in the ordinary form.
I do not think the hon. minister gave any explanation in regard to the Bill.
Yes I did.

1 regret that I was not present when the hon. gentleman introduced his Bill, but I trust we will get some information in reference to it when the Bill is again introduced. The hon. minister seems to have been guilty of the very wonderful mistake for a farmer, of practically putting the cart before the horse when ln>
introduced a Bill first and had it read in the House, and then this afternoon brings in a resolution on which he founds that Bill. I do not suppose it will be necessary to go through the form of reintroducing the Bill, but it struck me as rather peculiar that some hon. gentlemen did not take exception to it, and hold the Minister of Agriculture to the same rule that was meted out to the hon. member for Montreal (Mr. Bicker-dike) on his Cigarette Bill. This Bill will have to be very carefully dealt with. There is a great deal of danger in having so much inspection. It certainly would be of benefit to the farming community to get seeds free from all kind of adulteration, but I rather fear that it is dangerous to inflict these large penalties for such slight infringements of the law as the difference between 81 per cent of purity and 79 per cent. I am not sure from the wording of the Bill whether it applies to the farmer who grows the seed and who sells it to the dealer in the first instance.
It does not.

I have read the sixth clause which refers to that, but the same question comes up here as came up in connection with the last resolution we considered. One person may sell butter to another not Intending it for export, but the purchaser may afterwards export it; and so the farmer may sell seed to a merchant not knowing whether it is going to be recleaned or not. If it is recleaned he would not be liable for the penalty, but if it is not recleaned there is a danger that he may be made liable.
That is not the intention of the clause.
All these things will have to be very fully considered.
Hear, hear.

The farmer must have his apples inspected and he must have his butter inspected, and now he must have his seeds inspected. I do not find fault with these laws, but before putting them on the statute-book they should be well thought
out. I rather fear that such legislation Is going to open the, door to the appointment of persons to be inspectors of one thing or another, just as in the case of binder twine. I trust that these various Bills are not passed simply for the purpose of giving positions to the friends of tile government.

I can assure my hon. friend that the Bills are not promoted for that purpose. There is no intention of appointing an inspector with regard to the butter, but, although I cannot say positively, there may have to be an inspector or two appointed under this Bill. The farmers in the country have for years complained of the quality of seeds they purchased, first because of the number of weed seeds among them, and in the second place, because frequently the seeds are not found to be matured and germin-able. For many years individual farmers have sent seeds to the experimental farm to be tested, and the report was sent to the individual and was of no public utility. These complaints became so frequent that I instructed certain officers in my department under Prof. Robertson to start an investigation into the trade in seeds and the results were so startling that that investigation was extended. We found that farmers were imposed upon either by people who are selling inferior seeds, or through their own desire to obtain cheap seeds. We obtained a mass of information which was published in the bulletin issued by the department last year. I took advantage of the gatherings of farmers .last fall and winter to ask the speakers at meetings to discuss this question, and as a result we have had a large number of requests that we should protect the farmer in this respect. This Bill embodies what seems to be necessary to protect the purchaser of seeds in Canada. I do not say that the Bill is perfect. It is a difficult problem to deal with, and it requires the closest scrutiny, as my hon. friend from Halton has said. My officers before drawing up this Bill discussed the matter with the seed dealers and with the various agricultural bodies and I hope that with the thorough ventilation which the discussion of a Bill like this ougjjt to receive in the House (and I invite the fullest investigation and discussion of every detail of the Bill) that we may be able to find a solution of the difficulties which surround the seed trade in Canada. It is only when we have found that solution that I desire to make the necessary enactment which will carry out the full and matured judgment of the House.

It is desirable I think that this resolution should pass ; and probably without that extended discussion that we have had on the resolution with reference to process butter. It is, however, important to know definitely from the minister to what extent the farming community have

expressed a desire for legislation upon this matter. The farmers know better than anybody else whether they need this legislation or not. I have not heard from the Minister of Agriculture whether there has been an expression of opinion by a majority of the farmers of Canada for legislation along this line. If there has been, then It is right that we shall have legislation ; but I am inclined to think it will be found that there has'not been anything like a universal expression of opinion in favour of legislation on the subject of seeds. I am clearly of opinion-and I hope I shall be able to press this view on the attention of the House from time to time-that we are too apt hastily to introduce legislation of this kind. I do not think we sufficiently appreciate the fact that the farmers of Canada are quite capable of looking after some of their own business themselves ; and I think there has been too great a tendency, not only in this parliament, but in other legislatures, to interfere with the farmer and treat him as if he ought to be in leading strings, and if his conduct required to be regulated. This measure, as has been said, necessitates an inspection, and inspection entails expense and patronage and other evils which do not result beneficially to the farming community. I am not at all opposed to this resolution passing; but I want before the Act passes, to have some definite statement from the minister, and some indication from the farming community as to their will in the matter.

I regard the Bill before the House as one of the most important that we have had before us for a long time. When the government presents a railway Bill involving the expediture of millions of dollars it is regarded as a very important matter. But when a Bill of this kind comes before us, it appears trivial; and yet associated with it are facts of such tremendous consequence that it is very important that we should consider it carefully and deliberately. This Bill is intended to prevent the fouling of the soil throughout the length and breadth of this country. I am surprised when I go through the country to see the number of farms completely covered with noxious weeds, which could have been entirely prevented if the care which we now intend to exercise had been exercised ten or fifteen years ago. The mere fact that the farming community have not asked for this Bill does not prove that the necessity for it does not exist. I am surprised at the ignorance which exists throughout this country upon the subject of seeds. That was brought to my attention a short time ago by a visit which I paid to the seed experimental station which we have in Ottawa. The necessity for this very Bill was there strongly impressed upon my mindi. Farmers often buy seeds at $5 or $6 a bushel when they are really paying about $30 a bushel for the fertile seeds; they be-Mr. LENNOX.
ing loaded with twenty or thirty varieties of noxious weeds. It is to prevent this that this Bill is introduced; and before it passes the final stage, it would be well for hon. gentlemen who are interested in the matter to visit the seed-inspecting station and acquaint themselves with what this Bill is intended to do for the country.

House again in committee on the proposed resolutions (page 4363) regarding aid to the Canadian Northern Railway Company.	.
On resolution 2,

I observe that some words have been left out at the end of this resolution- I do not know whether in the copying in my office or as I received the resolution from the Department of Justice-which leaves it in a very incomplete form. You will observe that the resolution reads :	Provided
also that the said mortgage shall be a charge next after a first charge of $13,000 per mile (to be created by the company) on that part of the said Prince Albert Branch. But the description of the part is left out, and I propose to add these words: From the eastern end of the 100 miles hereby aided to Erwood.
speakername: The MINISTER OP RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Would it not be practicable to provide in these resolutions that the company, whose bonds are to be guaranteed by the government, should pay a larger rate of interest than that at which the government borrows the money ? The company could not borrow at less than 4 per cent, and it would not be unreasonable, in. view of the responsibility we assume, to ask that it should pay that rate for the use of the money. If that course were pursued, the government could invest the 1 per cent as a sinking fund, and in the course of fifty years the accumulations would wipe out the indebtedness. It would not be a hardship to the promoters to be asked to pay interest at the rate at 4 per cent, and provision might be made that the sum at the credit of tbe sinking fund should be handed over to them whenever they were prepared to relieve the government from the responsibility. I would like to ask the hon. minister if he has considered the advisability of such a provision ?

The hon. member will observe that what we are here doing is to provide a government guarantee on bonds to be issued by this company bearing 3 per cent interest. If the government were to conclude to charge an additional rate to the company, they would do that, not in these bonds, but in the further mortgage security contract, or arrangement that might be made with the company. It would not answer to place the rate at 4 per cent in these resolutions, because the bonds we are guaranteeing bear interest at the rate of 3 per cent, and to do what the hon. gentleman suggests would probably place the value of the bonds at a premium, which would not be very-advisable. I am free to say that it would be quite open for us later, as perhaps one of the conditions to 160
be embodied in the general mortgage which we propose to take upon all the undertakings of the company-it would be open for us, if thought desirable, to put in that document such a clause as the hon. member suggested, and I would ask him to raise that point when the Bill is before the House.
speakername: The MINISTER OP RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: The reason I asked the hon. minister for information on that point is because when this matter was first discussed throughout the corridors and about the House, I understood that what the government intended doing was to guarantee the interest for a period of years on a certain sum of money per mile. But I find in the fifth clause that the government assume responsibility for the principal as well as the interest. That is a different proposition altogether. I think it goes without saying that the government can borrow the money at 3 per cent, and it would not be unreasonable to make the proprietors of the road pay 4 per cent. Suppose the government advanced $9,000,000 for the purposes of construction, on an annual payment of 4 per cent interest, the government, borrowing money at 3 per cent, would have $90,000 per year to dispose of, which, invested annually, in fifty years would amount to more than sufficient to wipe out the debt. I would just as soon see the government borrow the $9,000,000 and hand it over according as the work of construction proceeded, on such terms as I have taken the liberty of suggesting.
I do not know where Erwood is. But if I understood rightly the branch from Prince Albert to where it joins the main line is about 180 miles in length.
About that.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: On which the government guarantee $13,000 per mile for 100 miles, and that the road on which this guarantee is to be given is to be built from Prince Albert towards the point of junction. That is the 100 miles which is aided by the government. Is Erwood at the end of the 100 miles or the point of departure from the Canadian Northern Railway ?

Erwood is now the terminus of what is known as the Prince Albert Branch and is 180 miles from Prince Albert. There is an intervening mileage there of eighty miles between the easterly point to which we are aiding the railway from Prince Albert and Erwood. Upon those eighty miles the company will be free to make its line as a first charge up to $13,000 per mile.
speakername: The MINISTER OP RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: The hon. minister has the location of the road in his department ?
It runs almost due west.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: And the location from Prince Albert down to the point of junction ? Could he tell what the gradients and curvatures going east and west of the proposed line are going to be-the maximum?
I do not think it is more than one-half of 1 per cent-not quite that.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: If I remember rightly, we made it a condition on the Canadian Pacific Railway from Winnipeg to Lake Superior that the gradients should not be greater than twenty-six feet to the mile one way and fifty-two feet the other way. It is very important in the construction of a railway, which is intended to carry freight cheaply, that the gradients and curvatures should be provided and put in the contract by the government.
We are going to do that.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
What is the reason for the provision in the latter part of the second section ?	' Shall be a first
charge next after a first charge of $13,000 per mile (to be created by the company) on that part of the said Prince Albert Branch from the eastern end of the 100 miles hereby aided to Erwood.'

They must be afforded some opportunity to raise the money with which to construct this eighty miles-assuming it to be eighty, which is as nearly as I can state the number. They are getting no government aid, the hon. gentleman will observe, and they have to build eighty miles, and when they do build they will require to encumber to the extent of $13,000 per mile.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Have they authority to do that ?
Yes, they have power under their general Act. I trust I make myself clear.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I think, I must have missed something that the hon. gentleman said before, for I do not understand the matter yet. The government are to guarantee bonds for 720 miles of railway, roughly speaking. Is it a portion of that 720 miles ?

And the eighty miles farther west ? No, there is no part of that. Perhaps I might make it a little clearer to my hon. friend (Mr. Borden, Halifax). The government is more concerned as to the building of the 100 miles eastwardly from Prince Albert than as to the building of the 80 miles further to carry it to Erwood, for the reason that there Is a continuous and growing settlement, a settlement of long stand-Hon. Mr. HAGGART.
ing, extending along this line, for 90 odd miles. The government has been so pressed by the people who have been looking for a railway in that locality that we have felt ourselves justified in making provision whereby that stretch of 100 miles should be promptly built. And we understand from the company that it is their intention as speedily as possible not only to complete that 100 miles which they contract with us to build, but to complete the other 80 miles, making the connection complete from Erwood to Prince Albert-completing the Prince Albert branch so called. We have, therefore, left the opening to enable them to place a mortgage to the extent of $13,000 a mile upon this 80 miles. When they are in a position to do it they will go on with the work, but, in the meantime, subject to that reserve right to them, we take an encumbrance covering the whole, the same as we do the rest of the undertaking.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: If the settlers in that section are anxious to have the road why does the hon. minister make the line of railway complete from the main line, instead of being built from Prince Albert 100 miles down, and leave them with an 80 mile gap reaching from the main line. And, while I am on my feet, I would ask, is there any subsidy in land or money from the local government or this government on this 80 miles of road ?

No. The hon. gentleman will recollect the fact that this mileage is all in the North-west and none of it in Manitoba. They are not getting any land grant for the line from Erwood west to Prince Albert. We are giving them no aid whatever except what is provided in these resolutions.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I did not mean from Erwood to Prince Albert but from Erwood to the main line.
They have it complete to Erwood.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I see. The hon. minister promised, when this matter was last under discussion to lay on the Table a statement showing the extent of road of the Canadian Northern already built, and the amount of rolling stock on the road that is to be given as further security for the advance proposed by these resolutions.

Of course, the hon. gentleman understands that that is information not in my possession ; I can only give It as it may be furnished me. I shall not be able to have it to day, but I will have it by the time the Bill comes up.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
That will do perfectly well, if the hon. gentleman will have it the day before the Bill is introduced,

and also a map showing the location of the Canadian Northern and this branch
Does the hon. gentleman mean the branch from the main line ?
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Yes, the main line and the branch to Prince Albert, that the hon. gentleman proposes to subsidize. We wish to see it on the map.
I think that, perhaps. I could manage to bring a small sketch map.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: That will do.

The hon. gentleman (Hon. Mr. Haggart) is, perhaps not aware that the Swan River section was at one time supposed to be intended as the main line, and when they made that line to Erwood and started to build to Prince Albert, it was expected that that line would be continued on to Edmonton. But, two or three years ago a change was made in their plans. A shorter route to Edmonton has been determined upon. They start out from Grandview and build direct to Edmonton.

House in committee on Bill (No. 131) to incorporate the Marconi Wireless Telegraph Company of Canada, Limited.-Mr. Mc-Isaae.
On section 24,

I call the attention of the Minister of Finance and the Minister of Railways to the wording of this section. This company is formed under section 15, to conduct the business of telegraphic communication not only by wireless, but by any other system, and by section 24 this company is authorized to acquire and deal with the capital stock, shares and so on, of any corporation having objects similar to the objects of this company. The telegraph companies of Canada are just as important as regards monopolies as any other corporation, and hence this section is of very great importance. I think it is time that the government should take care that clauses are 'not inserted in Bills of this kind that are likely to, or may create monopolies. The question arose years ago with regard to railways. It was found that when the parliament of Canada inserted provisions in various charters to prevent one railway 160}
company from absorbing another, shrewd business men soon found that it was quite possible to get the control of another railway without any absorption of it. By acquiring a majority of the stock and electing a board of directors a railway company desiring to monopolize the business of the country could just as effectively control the competing company as if it were actually amalgamated by Act of parliament. Everything that applies to railway companies in that respect applies equally to telegraph companies. It may be all very well for gentlemen to think that the Marconi system is confined to wireless telegraphy, but section 15 provides that they can carry on the business of wireless telegraphy or telegraphy by any other system.
Section 15 was struck out of the Bill.
Even if it is struck out, why should this company have power to acquire the stock of any other company chartered for similar purposes ?
It is put in every charter.

In the Railway Act, by section 276, no railway company can employ any of its funds for the acquisition of stock in another railway company, and by section 277, a heavy penalty is imposed upon the directors of any railway company which authorizes the purchase of stock in the shares of another company. What is the distinction between a telegraph company and a railway company, so far as the public utility is concerned ? I contend, as a matter of principle, that any company that is created by this parliament for the purpose of any public utility should not be authorized by a general provision of this kind to acquire the control of another company of a similar character.

This subject was fully discussed before the Railway Committee in connection with this Bill, and it was not the opinion of the committee that the clause was objectionable. After all, it is only a question of means. If any company has the means to obtain control of the stock of another company, it could accomplish its aim indirectly, if not directly. It is practically impossible, by any known method of legislation, to prevent that sort of thing being done. But after all, is there any reason why there should be a positive bar placed against a combination of two or three telegraph companies if they wish to combine ? They are not monopolies in a vefy large sense, but only in a very limited sense. My hon. friend puts them upon the same footing as railways, but there is a broad distinction. You can multiply telegraph lines, but not railways. You can not lay railways down and operate them without covering a good deal of ground, and without very seriously interfering with

the public, and the use of property in various ways. But telegraph lines may be strung all over the country and no serious hazards would arise or injury be done. It was not thought in the committee that there was any sound objection against allowing the clause to pass, particularly as it is one which is almost invariably included in any Bill which is granted for the same purposes as this.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
I would like to say, in answer to the hon. member for Ottawa, that when I said section 15, I was mistaken in the number, and what I intended referring to is section 12, which allows this company to carry on the business of telegraphic communication by means of wireless or other system of telegraph. This covers all telegraphic business of any kind in the Dominion. With regard to what the hon. Minister of Railways has said, I would reply that so desirable was it considered by parliament to prevent one railway company from acquiring the control of another by the purchase of its stock or the majority of its stock, that two clauses were inserted in the general Railway Act to prevent anything of the kind being done unless in particular instances expressely authorized by statute. These clauses were passed after full consideration and after a great many evils had occurred in this country through the acquisition and control of one railway by another, contrary to the intention of the Dominion and provincial legislatures. Section 276 of the Railway Act expressly provides that no railway company shall expend its funds in the acquisition of the shares of any other railway ; and in order to get over the difficulty which the hon. Minister of Railways has pointed out, this provision was put in the Act:
Every director of a railway company who knowingly permits the funds of any such company to be applied in violation of the next preceding sections shall incur a penalty (f $1,000 for each such violation.
Therefore, every railway director who authorizes the purchase of a share of stock in any other railway company renders himself liable to a fine of $1,000. It was a serious evil which caused such a provision to be inserted in the general Railway Act ; and when we are considering Bills of this kind-whether dealing with railways, telegraphs or telephones, and we have heard lately a great deal about telegraphs and telephones-we should take care not to authorize what is so particularly guarded against in the Railway Act.

There is a difference of opinion on the subject, and the hon. gentleman is entitled to his opinion, but other people are equally entitled to theirs. I did not; suggest that, in the face of that clause in the Railway Act which the hon. gentleman has read, a railway company could out of its own Hon. Mr. BLAIR.
means buy stock in any other company, but I did say that in this particular case there are large and wealthy stockholders who, if they felt that it would be a very great advantage to them to acquire the control of one or more telegraph companies, could take their means and buy the stock and operate these other companies in co-operation with the one we are now incorporating. There is no law you could pass which would prevent that being done. It is only one remove farther away. If these things are in the interest of capitalists, they will accomplish them in spite of any legislation we can pass. It is quite true that the Railway Act contains a general clause of the character the hon. gentleman has stated, but while that is the case, what do we find ? There is not a Bill that comes up for the incorporation of a railway company in which we do not find a clause authorizing the acquiring of other roads.

speechtext: By name. The hon. gentleman insists in every case that the name of the company to be acquired shall be put in the Bill, so that the committee may consider whether that particular company shall be amalgamated or not.

That is true, but all the same there is the general Act which imposes a penalty for doing that. I think, without a single exception, where the other company can be named, the company wishing to purchase is allowed to do so. There are only, after all, one or two great institutions which we would not allow to combine their interests. It is thought to be in the general interests that the larger roads should buy up the smaller ones, because they can work them to better advantage, give better service and afford better accommodation to the general public. In the case of the wireless company now under discussion, it became clear to the committee that Mr. Marconi might find it necessary, in order to give the public a better service, to make connections with telegraph lines. One can very well conceive that there might he obstacles raised to their working unless they had the power of using their means to obtain the control of some other lines which they could connect with their ocean cables, and it would be very unwise for us to say that they should not do any other business than a wireless telegraph business. They might, in the ordinary course, require to do ordinary telegraph business. The extent to which they can do that you cannot very well limit. But you can scarcely conceive of their going in to buy out all the telegraphs of Canada. If they failed to give the public a satisfactory service, how long would it be before other telegraph companies would be incorporated and compete with them for public patronage ? I think that we are magnifying the possibility of any ill effects resulting from legislation of this kind. While I would not hesi-

tate to place every obstacle in the way of any amalgamation of these great interests which could be detrimental to the public interest, I do not see why we should place any obstacle in the way, when the result would not be harmful.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: If we do allow amalgamation, it seems to me that we should make provision to prevent what takes place every day in connection with the two telegraph companies which amalgamated in Canada some years ago ; I refer to the Dominion and the Montreal Telegraph Companies. The Dominion line was projected for the purpose of giving competition to the public. It succeeded for a length of time, but getting somewhat financially embar-assed, the- Montreal Company got control of it, and what has been the result ? One company now controls the lines of both companies and does the work of both. But if you wish to send a message to a certain point, and go to the office of the Montreal Company you are told that the office at the other point is a Dominion office. The result is although one company controls both offices and manages both, you have to pay a double rate, because you are told that the message has to go over both lines. Had these companies remained separate, there is no doubt that both companies would have offices at these various places, and you would save the double expense which is now incurred. It seems to me that there ought to be some provision to prevent that kind of thing. That is one of the evils that result from amalgamation.

When this Bill was before the Railway Committee, it was very carefully considered, especially this clause in its bearing on the other parts of the Bill. At the suggestion of some members of the committee, certain words in this clause were struck out, so that it was left in exactly the same shape as the clauses usually put in Bills of this sort. There was before the House last session a Bill relating to the Canadian Northern Telegraph Company. It was very vigorously contested by many members of this House, and it was referred by the Railway Committee to a sub-committee. There it was considered and discussed, and finally it was reported to this House ; and that Bill contains exactly the same clause as this. I understand that it is a rule of the House, when a Bill is reported from the Railway Committee, not to disturb it unless for some very good reason. If we have granted a similar clause to other companies, I do not see why it should not be granted to this one. I do not apprehend any of the difficulties which the hon. member for Hamilton suggests, and I agree with the hon. Minister of Railways that it is absolutely impossible to prevent the amalgamation of these companies. I think we might very well adopt a model clause on this point, and apply it to every company.

I hardly agree with the view entertained by the minister that because you cannot prevent one company controlling another, that is a good reason why this clause should be retained. Of course, you cannot prevent men getting stock in different companies, and in that way controlling them ; but if that control cannot be prevented by legislation, that is no reason you should expressly authorize something still worse. A director of one company may acquire a controlling interest in another, but that is a very different thing from the case where the company of which he is a director obtains such control ; and the very best reason against the hon. gentlemans argument is the general clause to which he refers. What is the use of having that clause in the statute if the hon. gentleman's argument is correct ? If it is a sound argument, it is a good ground for striking out the clause in another measure that we were discussing at six o'clock for preventing the Canadian Northern Railway from amalgamating with the Canadian Pacific Railway ; but I can scarcely think he would use that as an argument for eliminating that clause. 1 think the point to which the hon. member for Hamilton has drawn attention, is a very important one, and the committee should pause before assenting to a clause of that kind in this Bill.

I would like to call the attention of the minister to section 22. That seems to give power to the company to enter upon lands and take possession of them without in the first place paying compensation. Is it desirable to give these special powers of expropriation ? Why would it not be better in all these cases to refer to the terms of the General Expropriation Act. There is such an Act on the statute-book, or there used to be. I know there was a good deal of amendment to the Act in connection with the establishment of the Exchequer Court, but surely the Act itself remains. Why is it necessary to give these special powers of expropriation to these companies ? Will the hon. minister say that the rights of landowners are properly preserved under this section ? The company may enter into possession of the land without giving any security, and have the question of compensation determined afterwards. That is not very fair to the landowners. The general rule of expropriation is that the compensation shall be fixed and the money paid into court before the company expropriating shall enter into possession of the land. The terms of this section are very comprehensive, and, though I have not had the opportunity of

reading it very carefully, I should think it gave power to enter upon lands and to pay afterwards, and payment need not be made until, in ease of disagreement, there has been an arbitration to fix the compensation.

The two clauses of section 22 as we have them here give powers that are to be found ordinarily in legislation of this character. I agree with what the hon. gentleman (Mr. Borden, Halifax) has said that they could be much improved, not only in the particulars to which he referred, but in others. But this has been the course of legislation. Two or three questions were referred to in the committee when the matter was pointed out, and this is one that we would probably do well to consider and have it provided for by some general legislation. I am not sure, but I think the same provision is in the Act relating to public works. I know they read the sections from other Acts.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: It is far better, It seems to me, both in the interest of the public and in the interest of the company that you should have a carefully thought out Act for the purpose of expropriation, and when any company comes to this parliament and asks to acquire lands by expropriation, let it be referred to the general Act for that purpose. It is not in the interests of the companies to confer powers in sections, such as these, that are not very carefully worded. They are fruitful in litigation, and sometimes may not be in the interest of the public, and result in general dissatisfaction. For my part, I do not see why reference could not have been made either to the Railway Act or to the Act now on the statute-book, called the Expropriation Act, where you could find much more carefully thought-out provisions than these expressed in section 22.

I do not know whether the general law controls under section 22, but, if not in my opinion, section 22 should not be sanctioned by this House. Under this section it is provided-
The new company may enter upon the lands of His Maiesty and of any person or corporation-
speakername: The POSTMASTER GENERAL (Hon. Sir William Mulock).

speechtext: ' His Majesty ' is struck out.

But the rest stands. So, section 22 would provide :
The new company may enter upon the lands of any person or corporation whatsoever, and survey the same, and set out and ascertain such parts thereof as it thinks necessary and proper for the construction and erection of the works of the new company or its lines of telegraph or system, and take possession of and use the same for such purpose.
And they can construct works and fell trees on the property. But I see no pro-

vision here requiring security for damages, tender in advance or any of the safeguards thrown around the owners of land when expropriation under the system is sought. Under the railway system, an order of court may be obtained authorizing possession in advance of payment, but only upon the court ordering security to be given. I sec no such security provided for in this Bill. For one, I could not sanction such a provision as this. This company may or may not be solvent; and I am dealing with it in the abstract. But I do not think we should sanction the principle oT any corporation or person taking away another's property without indemnifying him in advance. Who is going to look after the rights of individuals if this parliament does not ?

Talk about a carping policy, but that is a tu-penny ha-penny policy indeed. If these people do not get a railroad they will have to abandon their homes or go to some place where there is a railway. If the Canadian Pacific Railway do build a line there it will serve one portion of the country, but the road we have already serves a different portion of the country hundreds of miles away. This road which the government now propose to assist with a guarantee of bonds is to serve a different portion of the country entirely. The people have been there for a good many years, and they informed me, when I held a meeting there this year, that they had some grain stored in their granaries for three years, and if Alessrs. Mackenzie and Mann had not come there and bought some of it, they would have had to leave the country. If they do not get this road, they will not stay in that part of the country ; they will have to move out, though it is well known that this Carrot River valley is the finest and most fertile part of the whole country.
Do I understand the hon. gentleman to say that all the sections within ten' miles on each side of the railway are taken up ?
That is, the homesteads that are fit to take.
Does the hon. gentleman not think that ought to be sufficient guarantee to build a railway without going any further ?

If you can get them to do it. They cannot borrow money on that; but that is sufficient for the government to guarantee the bonds, because it shows that they will never be called on to pay one cent of interest. The settlers will get relief, and there will be no charge on the country.

I feel very friendly disposed towards this proposition. In view of the requirements of the western part of our country, I think it is absolutely necessary that additional railway accommodation should be provided; but I wish to tell the Minister of Railways and Canals, with the greatest possible respect, that I

have not yet been able, probably from lack of intelligence, to get this scheme into my mind. The other day when it was before the committee, we had to insist on the estimates of the railway engineers being placed before us. I think the minister also promised to bring down a map showing the location of the projected lines. We have what may be called a map, but it is not such a map as this committee should have before it to enable us to judge intelligently just what the scheme is. I am not opposing this resolution at all. I think that the firm! who are to receive this guarantee are worthy of the commendation and support of the people of Canada, and that in their struggle to construct a transcontinental line they should be reasonably assisted; but I think the proposition has beeii placed before us in anything but a businesslike shape, and if the discussion has been lengthened, it is not to impede the progress of the measure through the committee, but because members have been groping in the dark in their efforts to understand it. We shall have to give an account to our constituents of this measure, and as one member of the committee I must say that I have not been able, from the "discussion that has taken place, to inform myself as I think I should be informed in order to give an iidelligent vote upon it. I enter a protest against the meagre, half-baked way in which this matter is being presented to us. It is not fair to the committee or to those who have to give a vote upon a matter of such importance.

I do not know whether I shall succeed, but I will attempt to simplify the matter to the hon. gentleman. The Canadian Northern Railway commences at Port Arthur, which is its eastern terminus, and runs to Winnipeg, and from there to Portage la Prairie, and thence north-westward. Perhaps the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Roche) can tell us the exact distance from Portage la Prairie to the point where the road forks.
Thirty-five miles.

At this point the road diverges. One fork runs to Erwood through the extreme north-west corner of the province of Manitoba, a distance of probably 200 miles from the junction of the forks. The other fork runs to Grandview. The proposition before the House is that both of these forks be aided-the Erwood line to Prince Albert
Not to Prince Albert, but from Prince Albert for 100 miles to the east.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: The hon. gentleman is not very well posted.

I think the simpler way is to say that the Erwood line shall be extended to Prince Albert. The proposition is that the government shall aid the company in pushing the northern fork through to Prince Albert and the southern fork, which is spoken of as the main line, through to Edmonton.

I think the reason the committee has been misled is that the resolution has not been made plain enough. As the minister has explained it was the original intention to make this Erwood line the main line; but the company have made the Gilbert Plains line the main line because of its being shorter, and they have made the Erwood line a branch to Prince Albeit. I would ask the minister what estimate per mile has he that this road from Erwood will cost ?

speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I think that is a pretty high estimate for the construction of that line.
There is an expensive bridge

I am aware that Mr. Greeuway's government aided the Mackenzie & Mann roads through the province of Manitoba to the extent of $8,000 per mile. This aid extended for twenty oi thirty miles into the territories on this Erwood branch. Mr. Roblin, the present premier of Manitoba, has further aided Mac kenzie & Mann in the construction of branch lines in the province; and in granting that aid, he has had the aid which Mr Greenway granted to the line in the territories transferred to the province of Manitoba. Mackenzie & Mann are now appealing to the Dominion government for aid over this same line which Mr. Greenway's government'aided.
Did Mr. Greenway give any subsidy for the 100 miles east of Prince Albert ?
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: He guaranteed the bonds to the extent of $8,000 per mile on this same line west of the boundary line running towards Prince Albert for a distance of twenty or thirty miles.
That would leave about 180 miles,

Yes, I am not complaining of that. I am not complaining at all of the government aiding this line. But what I do say is, that the people of Prince Albert and the people of the Carrot River country between Prince Albert and Erwood are very desirous of railway accommodation; and I congratulate the Dominion government on imitating the Manitoba government in granting this kind of aid rather than aid in the form of a cash bonus or land grant. Since the provin-

cial government have granted aid to Messrs. Mann & Mackenzie in Manitoba and since the North-west Territories are not granted provincial or local autonomy and are not in a position to build their own road, it is the duty of this government to come to the relief of the North-west Territories and assist in constructing this line of railway. I am going to support these resolutions. I congratulate the government on utilizing a portion of this for rolling stock. The Mackenzie & Mann system had their bonds guaranteed during the past session of the provincial parliament to the extent of $10,000, which is $2,000 more than the other guarantee, but with the stipulation that the $2,000 of excess are to be applied towards the improvement of their rolling stock. Under the circumstances I will support the resolutions, particularly with the understanding that this government shall have absolute control of the rates.
This one hundred miles is to complete the line to Prince Albert, and the other is to extend the Gilbert Plains branch to Edmonton ?

Yes.
On resolution 3,
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I understand that the minister has presented to the House a statement of the present indebtedness on this line ?

Yes, I read it to the House and it is in ' Hansard.'
On resolution 4,
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Would the hon. minister give us some general information as to the terms of the mortgage in respect of the matters which I brought to his attention the other day ?

I have not gone into the subject of the precise details as to the mortgage. We shall of course follow what is usual and customary in such cases. There have been mortgages which have been given to the Manitoba government and there are other mortgages which have been perhaps given in other parts of Canada. We will see what these mortgages are like and come to a conclusion as soon as we can. But I have not, nor has the Department of Justice, which will have charge of that branch of the subject, given that matter any consideration yet. In a general way we propose to embody all the clauses necessary to have the guarantee secured on the property which belongs to this company- all its property of every kind and description. I do not think that I could give the hon. gentleman any information beyond that at present.
speakername: The SIINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: On resolution 5,
At the end of the fifty years the government is liable for the principal.
But it will have the property.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: It would be more satisfactory if some arrangement could be made for the extinction of the debt at the end of the fifty years. I brought that matter to the attention of the hon. minister this afternoon and he promised to consider it.

I am not unwilling to do so. It would not be in the interests of the country that the character of the road, its maintainance and betterment and the efficiency of the service, should be impaired by unduly enlarging the fixed charges on the undertaking in its early stages. It is very important that all the earnings they will be able to apply towards improving their road, increasing their equipment and otherwise adding to the efficiency of the road, should be devoted to these purposes, and the question of guarantee is not so urgent a matter as it appears to the hon. gentleman. However, I am quite free to say that his suggestion is worthy of consideration and it will receive the attention of the government.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Is this all the distance over which the firm of Mackenzie & Mann have asked for a guarantee of bonds, or have they made any request for a similar guarantee should their road be extended to the coast ? If this Grand Trunk Pacific Railway road should go through to the coast and be given a bonus or a guarantee on their bonds, in what position would that place the Canadian Northern '! There would then be two transcontinental lines-the Canadian Pacific Railway and The Grand Trunk Pacific Railway. In what position would the Canadian Northern Railway be then, because these men, Mann & Mackenzie, are the pioneers of the second transcontinental road, and although we may vote these resolutions through, we may be called on in a few days to grant a subsidy to the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway ?

I trust the hon. gentleman will not think I am discourteous, because I should be very sorry to appear so to my hon. friend, but I am bound to say that he has introduced so many ' ifs ' in his question that it is impossible for me to give a definite answer. Hypothetical questions are questions to which governments are not extremely anxious, under any circumstances, to reply, and this is a hypothetical question which has so many ' ifs ' in it, that I am unable to answer my hon. friend. There are so many suppositions in his question that it would not perhaps be of any advantage if I were able to reply, which I am not.

X may say, however, that there have been no negotiations whatever between the government and Messrs. Mackenzie & Mann, beyond what are to be found within these resolutions.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Would the government have any objection to add to these resolutions a guarantee of bonds through to the coast or would they support such a resolution if I were to propose it ?

If my hon. friend will allow me, I will say to him that we must have a proposition before us, before we can decide on it. I could not say what we would do in the event of somebody making an application, and consequently it would not be possible for me to answer my hon. friend's question, but I can assure him that no member of the government has had any such question under consideration, as far as I know.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Has this firm requested for a guarantee to the coast ?
There has been no communication of any kind at all in that connection.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Is it fair to ask if any negotiations have been going on between the government and any of the parties concerned looking to the absorption of the Mackenzie & Mann railways by the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway ?

I can only say that the hon. gentleman (Mr. Clarke) is as well informed as I am on that subject. He reads the newspapers ; and, if you can rely upon the newspapers' statements, evidently, there has been some attempt on the part of these corporations to approach one another; and, if you can rely on the newspapers, these attempts have failed.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Is the government a party ?
Not in the slightest degree.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: No pressure brought to bear upon the Mackenzie and Mann establishment to compel them to merge with the Grand Trunk Pacific 7
Not to my knowledge.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
My only desire in mentioning this was to point out that these men are Canadians and that they deserve great credit for the pioneer work they have done on this section of a transcontinental road. I believe that they can push the road through just as well as the Grand Trunk Pacific or any other people can, and in mentioning that this guarantee of bonds be extended through to the coast, it would be merely to protect these people in case that the Grand Trunk Pacific went through. I
think that this road is a good transcontinental road, if the government intend subsidizing a transcontinental road.
On section 6,
Resolved, that the rates and tolls to be charged for the transfer and carriage of freight and passengers upon the lines of railway so aided and upon the lines owned by the Canadian Northern Railway shall be under the control of the Governor in Council or of such authority, commission or tribunal as is designated or constituted under any Act of the parliament of Canada for the regulation or control of the business of railways.
What is the quality of this control 7 Is it different from what we have in the General Railway Act 7

The General Railway Act, or if the Railway Commission Bill passes, the Railway Commission Law, will certainly, I think, afford very ample control. But it is always thought desirable that we should embody it In the contract, simply by reason of its being part of the law of the land. A contractual relation would exist between the railway and the government with this incorporated in the contract.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Will the government have any power to limit the fixed charges, and, for that purpose to limit the capitalization, in order to make the control of rates of some use 7 If you could get the fixed charges down to a low figure that would be a very material element of control.
Parliament has already specified the quantity of bonds to be issued.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
What is the quantity ?
The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANA i,S. The hon. member (Mr. Puttee) will remember that a general Act passed this parliament bringing all the lines they had acquired and built under one control and management, called the Canadian Northern, and the capitalization on these lines is limited to $24,000,000, if my memory serves me well.	.

Would the hon. minister state whether, in his opinion, the Railway Committee which it is proposed to constitute will have the right, with regard to these lines w^e are aiding, to consider the matter and the amount of the aid in fixing the charges the company may levy upon the traffic 7

I think it would always be a matter within the discretion of the railway board to consider the cost of operation and maintenance, and generally the cost of carrying the traffic, and an element in that consideration, probably, would be what this road cost the company. They are going to be enabled to build the road with lower

fixed charges by reason of the government guarantee. I am not at all clear but that it would be proper for the Railway Commission to consider that as an element in deciding what would be a reasonable tariff.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Is there likely to arise any clash of authority between the Dominion and the provincial governments in reference to this matter of control of rates ? The hon. minister is aware that the provincial government exercises the control of rates over the road in the province of Manitoba. The rates on this line that is being extended into the territories would be under control of the Dominion government. The minister will see that there is a possibility of having some clash of authority.

I am not able to see why any conflict of authority should arise. The hon. member (Mr. Roche) will remember that when the Manitoba arrangement was brought up for the confirmation of this parliament, that question was discussed, and I think it was the opinion of both sides that no conflict of serious import could arise between the two authorities. If there should be a conflict, the government of Canada must prevail ; the decision of the Governor in Council must necessarily govern.
speakername: The MINISTER OP RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: With regard to the point I mentioned, let us suppose a case, a perfectly possible case. This Canadian Northern line will be built with public aid into Prince Albert. The Canadian Pacific Railway Company may carry the Manitoba and North Western Railway into Prince Albert, and, if so, we understand they will build into Prince Albert without aid. Would it be the duty of the commission to fix lower rates on the Canadian Northern on account of the aid given them than that they would fix on the Canadian Pacific, a road built without aid ?
The hon. gentleman (Mr. Scott) means without direct contribution from this parliament.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Without public aid.

It would hardly be correct to say that the Canadian Pacific is building without aid under all the circumstances. As a matter of fact, we know that enormous land sales are of great financial assistance to the company, and that has been a grant of aid to the Canadian Pacific. They are able to use the proceeds of these sales of land, which aggregate such large sums, to extend their branches and improve their road. So, practically, they are getting aid just as much as this company is, which is getting it in more direct form.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: What the minister says is that my supposititious case is not on all fours with the other. Well, let us suppose the ease of a road that is built without any public assistance as we understand it, and this road aided by the government. In that case, would it be the duty or the right of the commission to establish lower rates on one line than on the other, or should they fix equal rates on both lines ?

I would not like to undertake to define what the duty of the commission would be, except in a most general way. It would depend upon circumstances, and the circumstances would have to be weighed at the time the question arose and a decision arrived at according to the best judgment of those officials. I could not undertake to pass upon a matter which has not come up,-no facts, no circumstances, no material on which I could form an opinion.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I am not sure whether I understand this or not. The rate and tolls to be charged on this road are to be controlled by the government in some way. Does that apply to the whole line of railway, that is to all lines owned by the Canadian Northern ?
No doubt the resolution which is dealing simply with these miles of railway that are being aided, only applies to these lines.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
I think it applies to more than that. It says :
The rates and tolls to be charged for the transfer and carriage of freight and passengers upon the lines of railway so aided, and upon the lines owned by the Canadian Northern Railway, shall be under the control of the Governor in Council.
That would appear to cover the whole, would it not ?

Perhaps it would. The following words are somewhat broader than I thought they were. But there is now the same control over the other portions of the line. We have declared it, and we have conferred it upon the Board of Railway Commissioners as well. So that in every possible way, so far as general legislation goes, I think we have covered the ground.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: It does not add anything, I suppose, to the general law ?
No, only it becomes part of the contract.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
The clause in the contract between the Canadian Northern and the province of Manitoba is a little more explicit than this. It reads :

The Lieutenant Governor in Council shall from time to time fix the rates to be charged and demanded by the company for the carriage of all freight from all points of the companies' lines.
And so on.
Provided always that before any rates are so fixed the company shall be heard and their interests taken into consideration.
In one ease you have control ; In the other case there is an expressed provision that the Governor in Council shall fix the rates.
The commission will have power to fix the rates.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Will the minister say that the commission will actually exercise their power ? In Manitoba the rate on grain was fourteen cents per 100 pounds before that contract was made, and it has been reduced two cents per 100 pounds by the government. The premier has announced that another reduction of two cents per 100 pounds will go into effect after the 1st of July. So they are actually controlling the rates. The minister states that under this resolution the railway commission will have power, but will they exercise that power ?
I think it is proper to assume that in accordance with the object of our legislation they will exercise the powers which are conferred upon them in all proper cases.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: The hon. gentleman from Marquette (Mr. Roche) ought to explain the whole transaction. If there is a loss on the carriage of grain by the road by reason of the government having reduced the rates below the figure at which grain can be carried, the government of Manitoba have got to make good that loss on the earnings of that road every two years.

So far, I can assure the House and the hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. McCreary), the road is not being run at a loss. The best evidence is that the latest statements put forth by the company show that they have had a surplus every year, and the government has not been called upon thus far, and the premier states that he is confident they will not be called upon to pay a single cent of liability.

Of course, we know as much about it as the premier. If the country continues to produce such crops as we have had the last year or two there is no danger of any default. But let there be a short crop and there would be a danger. In the event of their being a shortage of crops for a year or two, there might be a default, and the government of Manitoba would have to pay. In that respect the resolutions now before the House differ from
those of the Manitoba government. I wanted to point out all the facts.

And I presume the hon. gentleman supported that contract.
On section 8,
Resolved, that it shall be unlawful for the Canadian Northern Railway to lease or sell any of its lines or any portion thereof to the Canadian Pacific Railway Company or to amalgamate with the said company or enter into any agreement with the said company whereby rates upon freight or passengers shall be pooled ; but this provision shall not extend to traffic or running arrangements made with the assent of the Governor in Council.

In reference to this clause, the minister stated in discussing this question yesterday that even if this road amalgamated with the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway it would be a benefit to that country, as it would then provide a second transcontinental line. As the hon. gentleman is aware, there are rumours at present, whether well founded or ill-founded, I do not know, pointing towards negotiations being carried on to have an amalgamation, or the taking over by the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway of the Mackenzie & Mann railway system. Now this clause specially debars this railway from being purchased or leased by the Canadian Pacific Railway. That is quite justifiable, and in the interest of that country. The people don't want to see this road fall into the hands of the Canadian Pacific Railway. They wish to see them kept separate, and they feel confident that in the future they will have plenty of produce for two or three transcontinental lines, and they do not desire any railway monopoly. But I feel confident that I am voicing the opinions of practically all the people of that country when I say that they are just as anxious that this road should not fall into the hands of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway. The minister stated that he Wished to see a second transcontinental line, and that this would possibly be the best way to secure it. I agree with him that an amalgamation would be desirable if it was at all probable that the Mackenzie & Mann were not able to carry through to a successful issue the prosecution of their enterprise. But thus far they have kept faith with the people of this country, they have shown themselves to be railway constructors, not railway exploiters. I wish to do that justice to them. In every respect they have kept their contracts with the provincial and Dominion governments, so far as the construction of their lines is concerned. Now what I fear, and what the people object to, is that if this road should fall into the hands of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway it will prevent the construction of a third transcontinental line. The Minister of Railways, in committee the other day, stated that if this charter was granted to

the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway their road would not be constructed within thirty miles of any other transcontinental main line. So that if the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway secure their charter, their road must traverse an entirely different section of the country and develop a portion of that country that will not be opened up by the Canadian Northern Railway or by the Canadian Pacific Railway. There must at least be thirty miles between the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway and the Canadian Pacific Railway or the Canadian Northern Railway. So I feel convinced that the people will object to an amalgamation or purchase of the Canadian Northern Railway system by the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway, though possibly not so much as they would object to an amalgamation with the Canadian Pacific Railway. We desire to see three transcontinental lines in the near future, there will be abundance of room for them. I fear that if we do not put a provision in here to prevent an amalgamation, either by the Canadian Pacific Railway or by any other railway that may be chartered by this parliament in future, probably we are going to create a regrettable condition of affairs, and that the government will see, when it is too late the error of their way, that they have been throwing this whole northern country under the control of one company instead of two or more distinct companies.
The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS ANI) CANALS. If the Canadian Northern line should be built through the Rockies, and if the Grand Trunk Pacific should be built through, they would have, either of them, or both of them, to come to parliament to get permission to unite or either to sell to the other. Parliament would then be in a position to judge whether or not it was judicious to allow any such transfer, or sale, or amalgamation, to take place. We have not either of these lines built through yet, and I think we need not give ourselves a great deal of undue concern upon that subject. If the Grand Trunk Pacific should be able to come to an understanding, if they desire to do so, and if there are efforts being made in that direction to-day, of which I have no present knowledge, they will have to come to an understanding before they proceed to build any portion of their railway at all. If they are going to get that line, they will get it at once, or they will not get it all. The moment they commence to construct another line through, there is an end to any attempt on their part to acquire the Canadian Northern. It would be only for the purpose of getting the benefit of the Canadian Northern business, locations and charters, that they would seek to become possessed of that system. I think we can make our minds perfectly free on that subject. I do not believe my hon. friend (Mr. Roche) will find that the contingency that he anticipates will arise.
Mr. ROCHE (Marquette),
If it should, the union cannot be effectuated until parliament so decides.
Why have the Canadian Pacific Railway specified ?
We had to put this in here so that we might have it in the form of an absolute contract and have a positive affirmation that they would not do so.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: That is just exactly why I say that we should guard against amalgamation with any road built in the future. The hon. gentleman could put in a general clause. Does the hon. minister not think himself, in view of his declaration to the House that he thought it would be a benefit if they did amalgamate with the Grand Trunk Pacific, that they will be inclined to take advantage of that declaration of a minister of the Crown and complete negotiations ? Afterwards coming to this parliament and seeking legislation authorizing them to amalgamate, feeling sure they will be ratified after this declaration on the part of the government.

I think the suggestion which the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Roche) has made is entirely impracticable. If we adopt it we will be cancelling a good deal of the private legislation that we have been putting through this session. I imagine that there must be half a dozen railway Bills that have gone through or are going through this session that provide specifically that the company being incorporated shall have the right to amalgamate with the Canadian Pacific Railway. There are also two or three cases, I think, or perhaps more, where it is provided that the company being incorporated may amalgamate with the Canadian Northern. I think the suggestion of the hon. gentleman is quite impracticable. Of course, it would be perfectly practicable to specify that this company shall never amalgamate with any company that may be incorporated under the name of the Grand Trunk Pacific, in the same way in which we are providing against amalgamating with the Canadian Pacific Railway. As a representative of the North-west, I may say that I think there would be a unanimous and very strong sentiment in that country against permitting the Canadian Northern to have the privilege of amalgamating with the Canalian Pacific Railway, but I doubt very much if there is one man out of a hundred who would have any feeling against a suggestion that the Canadian Northern and the Grand Trunk Pacific should amalgamate.

Then, the hon. gentleman takes the position that the people of the west only want one line.
On section 9,

The hon. Minister of Justice says

that In drafting the resolution the words ' subrogated in ' are used because that is the form in which they always use the term. With us, of course, it is quite different. We would use the expression ' subrogated to.'
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I am not wedded to that. That is the way our code uses It.

I do not get up for the purpose of criticising the language. In my own province we usually adopt the expression ' subrogated to.' In connection with the preparation of the mortgage, which we have not before the House, and as to Which I may say we have the very vaguest possible information from the hon. minister, if we could call it information at all-and I think I am paying a compliment to the hon. gentleman by suggesting that he has conveyed any information to the House or the committee-what will be your position if you adopt the scheme proposed by the hon. minister ? You will have these bonds guaranteed as to principal and interest by the government by some contract which will appear on the face of the bond, then you will have a mortgage, not indemnifying the government against its guarantee, but a mortgage to the trustee charging the principal and interest of these bonds upon the undertaking of the company. I suggest to the hon. minister that it would be better, from the standpoint of the government, and possibly no less in the interest of the company, to have a mortgage indemnifying the government against its guarantee, and I say that for this reason, which occurs to me at the moment: Suppose the company makes default in its interest, what is the position of tht government in case it should want to acquire the road or to exercise its rights, either by way of sale or otherwise 1 The government cannot take over the bonds, because the principal of these bonds is still vested in the persons who are the holders. The company is liable to these persons in respect to the principal of the bonds and it is liable to the government in respect to the interest on the bonds which is defaulted and which the government has been obliged to pay. It seems to me that it would be rather awkward to work that out in such a way that the government could exercise the rights which it ought to have in respect to foreclosing the mortgage. I dare say, of course, that it can be accomplished, but it would be a simpler course for the government to have a mortgage on the undertaking and property of the company indemnifying the government against any moneys which it might be called upon to pay under the terms of this guarantee. Of course, that is a question for my hon. friend the Minister of Justice when the document comes to be drawn.

I have not thought the matter out very much, but I apprehend that there would be given a second mortgage as it 101 [DOT]
were to the government which would practically be very much as the hon. gentleman suggests. Under that, the government could take any steps necessary to take possession of the property, subject of course to its liability for the bonded obligation.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: It adds nothing to the value of the bonds to prepare a mortgage such as the hon. gentleman suggests. Of course, if it would add to the security of the bonds it would be an answer to any observations I made on the subject, but inasmuch as the bonds are to have the whole security of the Dominion of Canada
That would be for our own protection.
