The question of jurisdiction with regard to the fisheries as between the Dominion government and the provincial government has been the subject of a decision of the Privy Council. That decision is not just as clear as the legal profession or even the Supreme Court would desire, and it would be very hazardous for any person in an off-hand way to attempt' to expound it. But I think it is conceded that there is joint jurisdiction. The Dominion government retains jurisdiction to a certain extent. It may, for example, pass regulations declaring under what conditions fishing may take place, and the provincial government may regulate the fishing in accordance with the general regulations prescribed by the Dominion government. That is, I think, as near as you can get to the meaning of the decision of the Privy Council. Under the division of jurisdiction, I think the provincial governments now appoint local officers, while it is still the duty of the Dominion government to see that its general regulations are observed by the local officers.

Why should the Dominion government be so anxious about that, and appoint a fishery inspector to carry out instructions which are so mystified that the Postmaster General can hardly understand them ? Then, how can a gentleman of Mr. Hurley's capabilities understand them ?
The hon. gentleman did not appreciate what I said.

If the hon. Postmaster General is coming to the rescue of the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries, I would ask him why should we expend so much money to inspect and be so anxious about the fisheries when they do not belong to us, and when the revenues derived from the use of the licenses go to the provincial exchequer ? The local government should be the party interested, and see that the regulations are carried out. That is the way it strikes me, and that is, I think, what any business government. - as this government claims to be, would say. The local government issues the licenses and gets all the money out of the job, and why should they not attend to the protection of the fisheries ?
The inspector appointed by the provincial government does not pass the regulations. The general policy for making use of the fisheries rests with the Dominion government.
Why ? When we do not get anything out of them ?

Why, is another question. For many years the Dominion government did issue the licenses and appointed the officers ; but in consequence of the decision in question, which gave a measure of jurisdiction to the provincial governments, the Dominion government has gradually ceased to exercise that control, leaving the provincial governments to do so. But the two governments work in harmony, the Dominion government having this policy, and the provincial government appointing the officers to see that the policy is maintained.

And getting the money.
THE POSTMASTER GENERAL. The officers appointed by the provincial government have not to construe the law. They have simply to see that the policy of the Dominion government is lived up to.

It looks to me not like a business proposition at all, and the hon. ter of Marine and Fisheries there are only three of these superintendents for the whole province. Mr. Hurley was a useful member of this House. If I remember rightly there was some discussion in the House with reference to Mr. Hurley last session. I think the hon. member for West Hastings (Mr. Porter) claimed that Mr. Hurley had arranged a protest against him through a Mr. Collins. As to the accusation made against Mr. Hurley, I think the hon. member for West Hastings (Mr. Porter) will admit, if he has not done so in the House before, that there in not the slightest foundation for the rumour that he had heard. Not only the other evidence, but the sworn testimony of both parties was taken to the effect that they had never made any agreement or even spoken about the matter-that they had had nothing to do with it. Even if they had, I do not know what crime it would be, except that Mr. Hurley, occupying a public office should not be mixed up in politics. Criticisms of the conduct of our officials is quite proper ; but when a man conducts himself properly and rumours injurious to him that are started are shown beyond all question to be entirely without foundation, I think that it is most unfair that those rumours should be repeated. As to Mr. Hurley's performance of the duties of the office, I can say that when I was in the department, I was assured by the officials that Mr. Hurley had' done faithful and effective service, and that there had been splendid results in his district, especially in the breeding of bass, car loads of which were sent to different parts of tlie country as far west as British Columbia-a very useful work, I believe. In view of the criticism I think it only fair to say that whatever duty has been assigned to Mr. Hurley he has conducted it faithfully and to the entire satisfaction of the head of his department. I am sorry again to hear, after this matter had been so clearly disposed of, that insinuations are made in regard to the same matter which was referred to on a previous occasion, based on a mere street rumour started by some evil-disposed person.

All I know about it is this : I happened to be speaking with the member for West Hastings (Mr. Porter) this evening, and he told me that this affidavit had been produced, and that since then this man Collins had told his partner that he had made an affidavit that Hurley did promise! him $100 and that he had got the $100 as agreed to from Hprley, notwithstanding the fact that Hnrley made this affidavit. Mr-. REID (Grenville). What earthly use is there in having these officers to supervise the fisheries, when the local legislature is making all the money out of it ? They are the parties who are interested. They have their own officers attending to that duty, and we are appointing officials to go over the same ground exactly. I suppose it is the duty of our officials to see that the officials of the legislature are doing their duty, but they are getting the money. I understand that

The hon. member need not listen to this if he does not wish to. I know that the inspector, Mr. Duncan, whom I am more particularly interested in, spends a great deal of his time in seeing that the nets are in the proper places and not on the spawning grounds, because if the nets were allowed to be placed there for fishing purposes the fish while spawning would be taken and the increase in the number of fish would be affected. I know also that he spends a good deal of his time, and with good results, in seeing that the Americans do not come over and fish about St. Joseph's island, Cockburn island and in the St. Mary's river. He has many a time chased these illegal fishermen out of the country, and, as far as he is concerned, I can assure the hon. member for Northumberland that his time is well spent, and that he earns every dollar that is paid to him.

I would recommend that the hon. gentleman be appointed Minister of Marine and Fisheries. He appears to know more about it than any of the ministers from whom I have asked information to-night.

Has the land been purchased ?

No. More ground is absolutely required there, and tbe intention is to buy part of a quarter section which is immediately east of the jail and we are getting it for $30 an acre, and I understand it is a great bargain at that price.
Mr. j^ENNOX. We are to understand that all these items can be discussed again on the main estimates ?
Yes.

Certainly, without any hesitation. I move that the committee rise, report progress, and ask leave to sit again. We have done a good evening's work, and I am much obliged to hon. gentlemen opposite for their courtesy.
Some resolutions reported.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE moved the adjournment of the House.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Will the hon. minister state what the business will be on Monday ?

Several Bills-one in the name of the Minister of Agriculture, and one in the name of the Minister of Justice, and then we will take up supply, disposing of tbe supplementary estimates if we can. We are more anxious to have them passed than the main estimates.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: The Railway Bill will not be taken up ?
It may be ; I am not prepared to say. We will take the minor Bills first, and if the Railway Bill is introduced later, it will be by agreement.
Motion agreed to, and the House adjourned at 10.40 p.m.
